newsitem.title: USA: AOL deal may cost few million dlrs in N.Y..
newsitem.headline: AOL deal may cost few million dlrs in N.Y..

text.p: New York Attorney General Dennis Vacco said that America Online Inc's settlement with several dozen states could cost AOL several million dollars for refunds to New York State's AOL subcribers alone.

Vacco did not have any exact figures on how much AOL will have to pay in refunds or credits as part of the settlement, but he estimated it could cost AOL up to several million dollars for New York state, depending on how many of New York's 600,000 AOL members seek a refund or a credit.
He also told a press conference in Manhattan that AOL has agreed to a one month advertising blackout in February.

"We calculate that the expanse of this deal for the 600,000 New York-based consumers will be well worth more than a million dollars -- probably in the few million dollar range," Vacco said at the news conference.

Vacco said that the settlement also required a black-out of AOL's television advertisements unless those ads include a disclaimer that on-line traffic jams may prevent customers from getting on-line with AOL.
He said that "anything that is already in the mill will continue to proceed, but they (AOL) will not initiate or will not continue any existing contracts that run through February."
If the adverstisement is in the pipeline and cannot be pulled, it will run with the disclaimer, he said.
Vacco said the settlement reached with AOL underlined the element of choice for the consumer.
Consumers could opt for pro-rated refunds or a month of credit, depending on the subscriber plan and the amount of time spent on-line.
For customers of the $9.95 a month metered plan, less than one hour online brings a full refund and one to three hours of service allows for a 50 percent refund.
The credit option allows customers to get one free month credit - "no questions asked."
Vacco said the agreement also calls for an improvement in the level of service.
Consumers will now have the ability to cancel their subscriptions by telephone, fax or mail.
For those customers who have pre-paid for service for one or more years, AOL will offer pro-rated refunds.
The cash refund option allows unlimited access customers to claim a full refund if they were online for two hours or less during December and January.
For those online between two and eight hours, a 50 percent refund will be offered, and a 25 percent refund for those online during those months for eight to 15 hours.

Service representatives will be increased to 4,600 from 4,000 and telephone callers who are put on hold will hear a message advising them of other ways in which they can be helped. Information about the agreement will also be
available online, Vacco said.

Vacco said that his office will continue to monitor the agreement and added that he was prepared to go ahead with a lawsuit if there was "slippage within the context of the promises made to the consumers in this agreement."
However, he said that the company "has shown absolutely no indications that there is going to be any slippage."
"I think it's a rock solid settlement," he said.
The settlement came just one day before Vacco was to file a lawsuit against AOL for allegedly deceptive business practices.

Eric Wenger, Assistant Attorney General, Consumer Frauds and Protection Bureau told Reuters that "in the final hour" before the afternoon conference, the Attorney General's office had learned, to their chagrin, that AOL's chairman Steve Case had decided to announce refunds separate from the agreeement.
Case had planned to "go across the board with a free month of service for all customers", which did not include cash refunds, Wenger said.
"There was a lot of pressure on the company," he said.
Final negotiations, which included persuading Case to stick within the parameters of the agreement, were only conluded minutes before the conference.
---Kamalakshi Mehta, New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610
